page.title: Inversion Basics
page.subtitle_html: Inversion Basics — B2 inversion after negative or limiting adverbials and not only patterns.
page.subtitle_text: B2 inversion after negative or limiting adverbials and not only patterns.

blocks.body: {"level":"B2","intro":"Inversion Basics: Inversion Basics explains B2 word order patterns such as never, rarely, only after, not until, and not only.","rules":[{"label":"Negative adverbials","text":"After never, rarely, seldom, or hardly, use auxiliary inversion.","example":"Never have I seen such a result."},{"label":"Only phrases","text":"After only + time or condition at the front, invert the main clause.","example":"Only after the meeting did we understand."},{"label":"Not only","text":"Use inversion after not only, then continue with but also.","example":"Not only did he apologize, but he also helped."}]}

page.title: Cleft Sentences Basics
page.subtitle_html: Cleft Sentences Basics — B2 cleft sentence patterns for emphasis with it-clefts and what-clefts.
page.subtitle_text: B2 cleft sentence patterns for emphasis with it-clefts and what-clefts.

blocks.body: {"level":"B2","intro":"Cleft Sentences Basics: Cleft Sentences Basics gives compact B2 anchors for emphasizing people, things, reasons, and actions.","rules":[{"label":"It-cleft","text":"Use it is / was + focused part + that / who clause.","example":"It was Anna who solved the problem."},{"label":"What-cleft","text":"Use what + clause + be + focused part.","example":"What I need is more time."},{"label":"Focus","text":"Choose the cleft pattern to highlight new or contrastive information.","example":"It was the timing that surprised us."}]}

page.title: Advanced Fronting And Emphasis
page.subtitle_html: Advanced Fronting And Emphasis - C2 fronted complements, locative inversion, negative fronting, and emphatic focus.
page.subtitle_text: C2 fronted complements, locative inversion, negative fronting, and emphatic focus.

blocks.body: {"level":"C2","intro":"Advanced fronting and emphasis: compact C2 anchors for moving information to the front of a sentence for focus and cohesion.","rules":[{"label":"Locative and complement fronting","text":"Front place, direction, or complement phrases when they carry discourse focus.","example":"At the heart of the problem lies a lack of trust."},{"label":"Negative and limiting focus","text":"Use fronted negative or limiting phrases carefully, with inversion where required by the structure.","example":"Only then did the implications become clear."},{"label":"Controlled emphasis","text":"Use fronting to highlight contrast, not as a decorative word-order change.","example":"What matters most is the reliability of the evidence."}]}
